# Trump rules out diesel export ban after Europe agrees to tap stockpiles
The president made the announcement hours after Europe caved to U.S.
pressure and agreed to release from its stockpiles of the fuel.
By [James Bikales](https://www.politico.com/staff/james-bikales)
10/02/2026 05:30 PM EDT

President Donald Trump said Friday he was ruling out a diesel export ban and never really considered one in the first place, hours after Europe caved to U.S.
pressure and [agreed to release fuel from its stockpiles](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/02/white-house-diesel-europe-01104936).
The announcement appears to put to rest more than a week of frantic lobbying across two continents after surging fuel prices — caused by the ongoing war against Iran as well as Ukrainian attacks against Russian refineries — have angered farmers and put pressure on the Trump administration to act ahead of the November midterm elections.
“Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a campaign trip.
“And we’re not going to be doing the export ban.
“It was never really ever on the table, but what Europe did was a great thing,” he added.
Trump had [repeatedly said](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/22/trump-decision-diesel-export-ban-soon-01087925) over the last two weeks that he was [open to suspending exports of the fuel](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/30/trump-diesel-export-ban-01101566), which would have been the first restriction on U.S.
energy exports since the Obama administration lifted a decades-old ban on oil exports in 2015.
The president [said just over a week ago](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/22/trump-decision-diesel-export-ban-soon-01087925) that “I’ve called for that” when asked about a possible ban.
But Energy Secretary Chris Wright and the president’s allies in the oil industry [publicly condemned the idea](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/white-house-ban-diesel-01089294), warning it could pose major economic problems for foreign countries who rely on U.S.
imports and eventually result in higher pump prices at home as refiners scaled back production.
Those advisers urged Trump instead to [push Europe to release fuel from its stockpiles](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/29/white-house-looking-to-europe-to-release-diesel-from-strategic-reserves-01096937), prompting a frantic public and private campaign of European governments by Trump administration officials.
The G-7 [announced Friday morning](https://www.politico.eu/article/trump-says-europe-agrees-to-release-massive-amount-of-diesel/) they would release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their strategic reserves over the next four months, beginning with a “frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.”
[POLITICO reported](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/02/white-house-diesel-europe-01104936) earlier Friday that the U.S.
had essentially strong-armed hesitant EU governments into releasing their diesel supplies with the threat of an export ban, with one European diplomat labeling it “blackmail.”
Trump told reporters Friday that he had “asked for” Europe to tap its stockpiles, but maintained that the Europeans had decided to tap their stockpiles out of their own volition.
“We have a very good relationship with Europe, and they wanted to do it because they have a lot of diesel,” Trump said.
“I said it would be great if you put it out to the markets, and they did it.”
The Trump administration could still announce further measures on diesel prices short of a ban next week, according to two people familiar with the discussions.
Among the ideas being evaluated are pushing more states to lift restrictions on red-dyed off-road diesel and suspend excise taxes on diesel sales.
*Meredith Lee Hill and Ben Lefebvre contributed reporting.*

The Trump Administration is pushing for a 90-day ban on diesel exports intended to rapidly lower climbing fuel prices for consumers, a proposal that, if enacted, will hurt the constellation of Texas refineries in the Gulf Coast and deal a blow to the state’s economy, industry leaders said.
*Politico* first [reported](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/white-house-ban-diesel-01089294) the news of the ban.
Texas refineries turn millions of barrels of crude oil into diesel and jet fuel daily for several industries, such as agriculture and aviation.
They also sell the product abroad.
Texas contributes about a third of the nation’s diesel, processing about 6.3 million barrels a day, according to the Energy Information Administration.
About 1.5 million barrels are sold overseas.
Now, the Trump administration is pushing companies to curtail such exports and keep that fuel at home to increase supply and lower volatile fuel prices amid the U.S.-Iran war, as rising gas prices become a political liability ahead of the November midterm elections.
On Monday, Gov.
Greg Abbott [issued a disaster declaration](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/28/texas-gas-diesel-prices-emergency-declaration-war-abbott/) that allows the use of dyed diesel, which is functionally the same as diesel but reserved in farming and construction, to ease prices.
The proposal has put President Donald Trump at odds with an industry he pledged to bolster by cutting regulation during his presidential campaign.
Curtailing exports, many in the industry fear, will force them to downsize operations and lessen supply.
Doing so could devastate parts of the energy sector, the bedrock of the Texas economy [that employs hundreds of thousands of workers and pays billions in taxes](https://www.txoga.org/2025eeir/).
“Banning exports of diesel would cripple domestic jobs, lead to fuel shortages here at home and put power in the hands of China and Russia by forcing our allies to turn to those countries to meet their needs,” said Todd Staples, president of the Texas Oil and Gas Association.
“America’s energy leadership is needed now more than ever, and the best way to protect Texas and American consumers is to encourage continued investment in infrastructure which means more production, pipelines, processing and refining.”
“Global disruptions to the supply chain will eventually be resolved and Texas will emerge stronger and consumers better protected than ever.
A ban today means a weaker America tomorrow and should be rejected by all Americans.”
CITGO, a major Texas refiner with operations in Lake Charles, Louisiana, and Corpus Christi, said it represents roughly 690,000 barrels a day of refining capacity, and it relies on domestic and international markets to balance production and maintain reliable operations.
“An immediate ban on diesel exports would eliminate outlets for approximately 1.3 million barrels-per-day of U.S.
diesel and create a significant product containment challenge across the U.S.
Gulf Coast, which supplies 90% of these exports,” a CITGO spokesperson said in a statement.
“The product containment challenge would force Gulf Coast refineries to reduce crude runs which, in turn, impacts overall fuel supply.”

CRS INSIGHT Prepared for Members and Committees of Congress INSIGHTi Diesel Export Ban: Transportation Policy Considerations for Congress October 1, 2026 On September 21, 2026, the average price of diesel fuel for use in highway vehicles reached $6.529 per gallon, according to the U.S.
Energy Information Administration.
In 2024, trucks and trains transported between two-thirds and three-quarters of all domestic freight (about 13 million of 17.7 million total tons transported), almost all using diesel-fueled engines.
Shippers of perishable goods, which cannot be easily stored for later shipment, may be especially sensitive to high fuel costs.
The Trump Administration and some Members of Congress are reportedly considering restrictions on the export of diesel fuel, with the goals of increasing domestic supply and reducing consumer product prices through lower shipping costs.
One such bill (H.R.
10423) would immediately ban exports of diesel fuel until the end of the calendar year.
Another (H.R.
10422) would automatically implement an export ban if the diesel fuel price averages more than $5.00 per gallon over a two-week period; the export ban would remain until the diesel fuel price was below $4.50 per gallon for 30 consecutive days.
The United States is a major exporter of diesel fuel.
If diesel fuel exports are restricted, refineries could be left with a temporary surplus, potentially leading to lower prices in the short term in some areas.
Fluctuations in the price of diesel fuel could present various surface, maritime, and aviation transportation policy issues for Congress to consider.
In response to a proposed export ban, industry analysts reportedly forecast that refineries could respond by reducing production of diesel until surpluses are depleted, depending on how any restrictions would be structured.
Diesel fuel is produced by refining crude oil in a process that also produces gasoline, aviation fuel, and other products.
A decline in the production of diesel could be accompanied by declines in the other types of fuel produced, potentially raising those prices depending on the overall supply and other factors.
In the global market, countries accustomed to importing diesel fuel from the United States would need to find other exporters at potentially higher prices.
For example, Mexico reportedly imports roughly 60% of its diesel from the United States.
U.S.
consumers may see higher prices for imported goods if diesel fuel costs rise in those countries.
Surface Transportation Railroads and trucking companies may respond to high diesel prices by internalizing additional costs and reducing profitability or by adding fuel surcharges to their base shipping rates.
Base rates are calculated assuming a certain price for diesel fuel, and surcharges (sometimes per mile, sometimes as a percentage Congressional Research Service https://crsreports.congress.gov IN12744 Congressional Research Service 2 of the base price) are calculated on the basis of how much the current price of diesel fuel exceeds the assumed price.
As of September 2026, fuel surcharges at some logistics companies are more than 25%.
Elevated diesel fuel prices could be contributing to a reported shift of freight traffic from truck to rail or intermodal (truck-and-rail) freight.
The transportation of cargo partly or entirely by train instead of by truck may allow shippers to reduce certain costs because of rail’s comparative fuel efficiency, though transport by trucks alone may reduce travel times.
Rail’s ability to carry additional cargo depends on the availability of railcars and locomotives and the capacity available at intermodal facilities where cargo can be loaded and unloaded.
Lower diesel fuel prices may reduce fuel surcharges, thereby reducing motivations to shift cargo movements from trucks to rail.
If elevated motor fuel prices were to cause a decline in consumption, such a decline could reduce the amount of fuel taxes collected by the federal government and deposited into the Highway Trust Fund, an important source of funding for many highway and public transportation projects.
Congress often considers fuel tax revenue and spending when it reauthorizes surface transportation programs (currently scheduled to expire on December 11, 2026) and could do so in upcoming surface transportation bills or through stand-alone legislation.
Maritime Transportation Fuel costs can also be an issue for maritime carriers.
Some barge tows are powered by diesel engines, and barges can be critical for agricultural shippers during the harvest season.
A diesel export ban may amplify calls to waive the Jones Act, which refers to provisions of law that require all waterborne shipments between U.S.
ports to be transported on vessels that are U.S.-built and U.S.-crewed.
By permitting port-to-port shipments of diesel fuel on foreign vessels, surpluses of diesel fuel might be more economically distributed to other markets in the United States not connected by pipelines that could help transport surplus diesel fuel.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a Jones Act waiver on March 17, 2026, shortly after military operations began against Iran.
DHS extended it twice, through mid-November 2026.
Of the more than 200 voyages taken under the March 17 Jones Act waiver as extended, over 20 carried diesel fuel according to reports published by the U.S.
Maritime Administration as of September 2026.
Aviation If refiners respond to a diesel export ban by reducing refinery output, the supply of kerosene-derived aviation fuel might lessen, increasing costs for airlines.
U.S.
airlines previously had pursued financial strategies to hedge against volatility in the price of aviation fuel.
U.S.
airlines reportedly have largely retreated from the practice in recent years, while European airlines have continued to hedge.
In response to higher fuel prices, airlines may raise passenger fares or freight rates, reduce capacity (i.e., offer fewer flights), reduce profitability, or some combination of these.
Congress could monitor fares and rates in the context of consumer choice and the national economy when considering how a diesel export ban might change aviation fuel prices.
Refiners may be able to shift production to increase the percentage of kerosene produced from each barrel of oil, which could offset lower production due to reduced oil processing.

# Diesel Export Ban Involves Transportation Policy Tradeoffs
By Legis1 Editorial· Edited by Carolyn Robinson, Joanne Levine
Tuesday, October 6, 2026· 2 min read
## Why It Matters
With average highway diesel prices at $6.529 per gallon on Sept.
21, according to the U.S.
Energy Information Administration, a [Congressional Research Service (CRS) report](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12744) says export restrictions could lower diesel prices in the short term in some areas and describes possible effects on surface, maritime, and aviation transportation.
The Trump administration and some members of Congress are reportedly considering export restrictions, with the stated goals of increasing domestic supply and lowering consumer prices through cheaper shipping costs.
The report, updated Oct.
1 and authored by Ben Goldman, analyst in transportation policy, does not endorse or reject a ban but maps the tradeoffs Congress would need to weigh.
The CRS report describes two bills: H.R.
10423, which would immediately ban diesel exports until the end of the calendar year, and H.R.
10422, which would automatically impose a ban if diesel averages more than $5.00 per gallon over a two-week period and keep it in place until the price is below $4.50 per gallon for 30 consecutive days.
## The Big Picture
In 2024, trucks and trains transported about 13 million of the 17.7 million total tons of domestic freight, almost all using diesel-fueled engines.
Shippers of perishable goods, which cannot be easily stored, may be especially sensitive to elevated fuel costs.
Industry analysts reportedly forecast that refineries could respond to an export ban by cutting diesel production until any surplus is depleted.
Because diesel is produced alongside gasoline and aviation fuel in the same refining process, a drop in diesel output could reduce supplies of those fuels as well, potentially raising their prices depending on broader market conditions.
Internationally, Mexico reportedly imports roughly 60 percent of its diesel from the United States, and higher fuel costs abroad could eventually raise prices for goods imported by U.S.
consumers.
The report also flags a Highway Trust Fund (HTF) complication, namely that if high fuel prices reduce consumption, federal fuel-tax receipts flowing into the HTF could decline.
Surface transportation programs are currently scheduled to expire Dec.
11, making that revenue question directly relevant to the upcoming reauthorization debate.
On the maritime side, the report notes that a diesel export ban may amplify calls to waive the Jones Act, which requires waterborne shipments between U.S.
ports to use U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed vessels.
The Department of Homeland Security issued a Jones Act waiver on March 17, shortly after military operations began against Iran, and extended it twice through mid-November 2026.
Of more than 200 voyages taken under that waiver, over 20 carried diesel fuel, according to U.S.
Maritime Administration reports as of September.
## The Bottom Line
The report identifies surface transportation reauthorization, Jones Act waiver policy, Highway Trust Fund revenue, and aviation fuel supply as issues a diesel export ban could touch, and it says the current surface transportation programs are scheduled to expire on December 11.

# Trump Says He Will Import Russian Diesel Fuel Amid High Prices
President Trump said Russia had agreed to ship potentially millions of tons of diesel fuel in the coming months.
But Russia has an ongoing ban on exporting diesel.
Reporting from Washington
President Trump said on Friday that he had reached an agreement with President Vladimir V.
Putin of Russia to immediately import Russian diesel fuel to the U.S.
market, despite a Russian ban on exporting fuel.
It was not immediately clear if Mr.
Putin had signed off on that deal.
But minutes after Mr.
Trump’s announcement, the Treasury Department said it was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports “to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market.” The announcement gave Russian energy producers a general license to sell diesel fuel until April.
Russia, a crucial supplier of diesel to the rest of the world, said last week that it was extending its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, amid punishing Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and other fuel infrastructure.
Those attacks, and the export ban, have kept fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections.
Mr.
Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for the strikes, saying they were driving up prices.
But Mr.
Trump said in a social media post on Friday that Mr.
Putin had approved shipping potentially millions of tons of diesel fuel in the coming months.
“It was agreed,” Mr.
Trump said, “that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter.
Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel.”
The return of Russian diesel to international markets would be a win for Mr.
Putin, who has sought for years to break the ice on U.S.
sanctions against Moscow’s energy sector.
Despite suffering from the most acute gasoline crisis in decades, Moscow still has an excess supply of diesel.
But Edward Fishman, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he doubted that Russia could supply as much diesel fuel as Mr.
Trump said it had promised.
“The reason Russia imposed an export ban was that Ukrainian strikes had degraded its refining output, necessitating fuel rationing for domestic use,” Mr.
Fishman said.
“This strikes me as classic Putin — empty promises aimed at sowing further divisions in the trans-Atlantic alliance.”
It is the latest effort by the Trump administration to ease sanctions on Russia in a bid to lower energy prices.
At the beginning of the war with Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent lifted sanctions on Russian oil that was at sea, saying that it would add hundreds of millions of barrels of crude to global markets, and would curb prices.
Alan Rappeportand Ivan Nechepurenkocontributed reporting.
Chris Cameron is a Times reporter covering Washington, focusing on breaking news and the Trump administration.

## Introduction
On 27 September 2026, President Donald Trump said that his administration was considering a possible diesel export ban “very seriously” and that it “may do it” (Bloomberg News, 2026).
No final export restriction had been announced by 28 September, while earlier reports of a flat 90-day prohibition had been denied.
The legal question is consequently prospective: WTO compatibility will depend on the measure actually adopted, including its duration, product coverage, geographic scope, and any exemptions.
The proposal arises against unusually tight conditions in the U.S.
distillate market.
The U.S.
Energy Information Administration reported that distillate fuel inventories had fallen below the 2021–2025 range in April and forecast that they would fall below 100 million barrels in September, remaining below the recent five-year low through the end of 2026 and for much of 2027.
Weekly stocks stood at approximately 107.4 million barrels on 18 September (EIA, 2026a; EIA, 2026b).
These figures document supply pressure, but they do not by themselves establish the treaty conditions required for an export restriction under WTO law.
Article XI:1 of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 1994 generally prohibits restrictions on the exportation or sale for export of goods other than duties, taxes, or other charges.
A blanket governmental prohibition on diesel exports would fall within the type of measure regulated by that provision.
Article XI:2(a), however, provides that Article XI:1 does not extend to export prohibitions or restrictions temporarily applied to prevent or relieve critical shortages of products essential to the exporting member (WTO, 1994).
The distinction is significant: Article XI:2(a) defines circumstances outside the prohibition in Article XI:1, while Article XX contains separate general exceptions subject to their own requirements.
The possible restriction also has direct implications for European energy trade.
On 24 September, the European Commission stated that it viewed the reported U.S.
plans with concern, confirmed that high-level contacts with Washington were underway, and said that there was no concrete shortage of diesel in the European Union at that time (European Commission, 2026).
The United Kingdom is separately exposed to changes in U.S.
supply.
In 2025, the United States supplied 31 percent of UK diesel imports, making it the largest individual foreign source, followed by the Netherlands and Belgium (DESNZ, 2026).
Other GATT provisions could become relevant depending on the design and justification of any U.S.
measure.
Article XX(j) concerns measures essential to the acquisition or distribution of products in “general or local short supply,” subject to the requirements of Article XX, while Article XIII governs the non-discriminatory administration of quantitative restrictions.
If Washington were to restrict exports to some destinations while maintaining them to others, Article XIII could assume particular importance.
Article XXI would present a different inquiry if the United States invoked the GATT security exception and relied on one of the circumstances specified in that provision (WTO, 1994).
The central legal issue is thus narrower than the political debate over fuel prices.
Market tightness may explain why export controls are under consideration, but WTO law imposes distinct conditions on restrictions justified by scarcity and separate disciplines on their administration.
Any eventual U.S.
measure would have to be assessed according to its actual terms and factual basis, with corresponding consequences for the European Union, the United Kingdom, and other WTO members affected by the restriction.
## 1.
Status of the Proposed US Diesel Export Restriction
The policy debate has developed in stages rather than through a single announced measure.
On 22 September 2026, President Donald Trump publicly supported the idea of restricting U.S.
diesel exports, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the administration was examining both full and partial restrictions (Reuters, 22 September 2026).
A day later, Politico reported that the administration was preparing a 90-day export ban.
The White House denied that a flat 90-day prohibition was being prepared, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that no such blanket ban was under consideration at that point.
He nonetheless acknowledged that the administration was considering ways to increase diesel availability in the domestic market (Reuters, 23 September 2026).
The issue remained unresolved.
On 27 September, Trump said that the administration was considering a diesel export ban “very seriously” and that “we may do it” (Bloomberg News, 27 September 2026).
By 28 September, no final measure had been publicly announced.
The form ultimately chosen would affect the WTO analysis.
A complete prohibition, a quantitative ceiling, a restrictive licensing arrangement, an export tax, or country-specific exemptions would not necessarily be governed in the same way.
The economic exposure is also significant outside the United States.
The European Commission has described the EU as a major importer of U.S.
diesel and expressed concern about possible restrictions, while the United States supplied 31 percent of UK diesel imports in 2025 (European Commission, 2026; DESNZ, 2026).
## 2.
GATT Article XI and a Diesel Export Ban
Article XI:1 of the GATT 1994 establishes the general prohibition on quantitative restrictions.
It bars WTO members from maintaining prohibitions or restrictions on imports or exports other than duties, taxes, or other charges, including measures made effective through quotas and import or export licenses (WTO, 1994).
The Appellate Body in China — Raw Materials interpreted Article XI:1 as covering measures that have a limiting effect on the quantity or amount of goods that may be imported or exported (WTO Appellate Body, 2012).
A direct prohibition on diesel exports would fall naturally within the concept of an export prohibition.
A quota restricting the volume available for export would likewise fall within Article XI:1, subject to the question of whether Article XI:2(a) removes the measure from the scope of that prohibition.
Fiscal measures are treated differently.
Article XI:1 expressly excludes duties, taxes, and other charges, so an export tax would not violate Article XI:1 merely because it makes foreign sales less attractive.
The legal classification of any U.S.
measure will consequently depend on the instrument actually adopted rather than on the political objective of retaining more diesel in the domestic market.
## 3.
Article XI:2(a) and Critical Shortages
Article XI:2(a) provides that Article XI:1 does not extend to export prohibitions or restrictions temporarily applied to prevent or relieve critical shortages of foodstuffs or other products essential to the exporting member (WTO, 1994).
Its operation depends on several linked elements: the product must be essential, the shortage must be critical or imminent, and the restriction must be temporary and directed toward preventing or relieving that shortage.
In China — Raw Materials, the Appellate Body interpreted an essential product as one that is absolutely indispensable or necessary to the member concerned.
It described a critical shortage as a deficiency reaching a stage of crisis or decisive importance, rather than ordinary scarcity.

# Atlas Analytics Forecasts 1.5% U.S.
GDP Growth in Q3 2026
### Following two strong quarters of forecasting accuracy, Atlas Analytics projects 1.5% U.S.
GDP growth in Q3 2026 despite trade headwinds.
[Jake Schneider](https://substack.com/@jakeschneider)
**The U.S.
economy continues to expand, but international trade is weighing on headline growth.** Atlas Analytics forecasts that real U.S.
GDP grew at a 1.5% annualized rate in the third quarter of 2026, down from 2.2% in Q2 and 2.5% in Q1.
Our latest forecast suggests that underlying domestic economic activity remains relatively healthy.
However, a widening trade deficit is expected to subtract substantially from headline GDP growth.
This forecast follows two consecutive quarters in which Atlas’s satellite-based GDP estimates came remarkably close to the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) figures.
## **Our Q3 2026 Forecast: 1.5% Growth**
Atlas Analytics’ final estimate for Q3 2026 is **1.5% annualized real GDP growth**, with three principal components:
* **Core GDP: +2.6 percentage points.** Private consumption, fixed investment, and government expenditures continue to support economic growth.
* **Private inventories: +0.5 percentage points.** Inventory accumulation is expected to make a modest positive contribution.
* **Net exports: −1.5 percentage points.** A widening trade deficit is expected to significantly offset domestic economic activity.
Together, these components produce our headline forecast of 1.5%.
The distinction between headline GDP and underlying domestic activity is particularly important this quarter.
Our forecast suggests that the U.S.
economy is growing more strongly domestically than the headline figure implies.
However, rising imports relative to exports are expected to weigh heavily on measured GDP.
Recent trade data reinforce this interpretation.
The U.S.
trade deficit widened sharply in August, with imports reaching record levels amid continued demand for industrial supplies, capital equipment, and technology-related investment.
In other words, weaker headline GDP growth does not necessarily indicate a comparable deterioration in domestic demand.
## **Two Consecutive Quarters of Accurate Forecasting**
Our Q3 forecast builds on encouraging results from the first half of 2026.
In Q1, Atlas forecast 2.04% GDP growth, compared with the BEA’s latest estimate of 2.49%.
In Q2, Atlas again forecast 1.95%, compared with the BEA’s latest estimate of 2.22%—a difference of just 0.27 percentage points.
Across these two quarters, **our average absolute forecasting error was just 0.36 percentage points**.
While two quarters represent a relatively small sample, these results are encouraging evidence of the potential for satellite-based economic forecasting.
Our objective is not simply to replicate traditional economic forecasts.
It is to develop an independent perspective on economic activity using alternative data sources that can complement conventional government statistics.
## **Forecasting the Economy from Outer Space**
At Atlas Analytics, we combine satellite imagery, geospatial information, and conventional economic data to develop timely estimates of economic activity.
Our approach seeks to identify real-world signals of production, transportation, consumption, and trade—often before these activities are fully reflected in official statistics.
This is particularly valuable when conventional economic indicators are incomplete, delayed, or subject to substantial revisions.
The third quarter illustrates why examining the individual components of GDP matters.
Our models suggest that domestic demand continues to expand, even as international trade reduces the overall growth rate.
## **What Comes Next?**
The BEA is scheduled to release its advance estimate of Q3 2026 GDP on **October 29, 2026**.
Our final forecast of 1.5% will provide another opportunity to evaluate how well our satellite-based approach anticipates official economic statistics.
Regardless of the outcome, our goal remains the same: to make economic forecasting more timely, transparent, and grounded in observable economic activity.
*Thank you for following Atlas Analytics as we continue developing a new approach to understanding the economy—from outer space.*
Atlas Analytics is a reader-supported publication.
To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).
In the first quarter, real GDP increased 2.5 percent (revised).
Real GDP was revised up 0.7 percentage point from the second estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government spending.

### GDP by industry
From an industry perspective, the increase in **real GDP** reflected [increases in **real value added** of 2.5 percent for private services-producing industries, 2.3 percent for private goods-producing industries, and less than 0.1 percent for government](https://apps.bea.gov/iTable/?reqid=1603&step=2&Categories=GDPxInd&isURI=1&_gl=1*1koyoax*_ga*NDE1NTUxNjIyLjE3NjQxNzQzOTE.*_ga_J4698JNNFT*czE3NzQzNjkzOTQkbzQ1JGcxJHQxNzc0MzY5OTMyJGo1NiRsMCRoMA..#eyJhcHBpZCI6MTYwMywic3RlcHMiOlsxLDIsNF0sImRhdGEiOltbImNhdGVnb3JpZXMiLCJHRFB4SW5kIl0sWyJUYWJsZV9MaXN0IiwiVFZBMTAxIl1dfQ==).

## What this release measures
Gross domestic product measures the value of final goods and services produced in the United States.
Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, while current-dollar GDP does not.
The headline quarterly growth rate is seasonally adjusted and annualized.
BEA also publishes details for consumer spending, investment, government spending, exports, and imports.
## Why the Federal Reserve watches it
GDP shows the broad pace of economic activity.
Strong or weak growth can change how policymakers judge demand, inflation pressure, and downside risks to employment.
The Fed does not set rates from GDP alone.
Policymakers compare output with inflation, labor-market data, financial conditions, and the composition and durability of growth.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### What did the latest GDP report show?
BEA estimated that real U.S.
GDP increased at a 2.2% annualized rate in Q2 2026, following a revised 2.5% increase in Q1.
The September 30 release was the third estimate and can be revised.
### When is the next GDP report?
As reviewed on October 2, 2026, the next GDP estimate is scheduled for Thursday, October 29, 2026 at 8:30 AM Eastern Time.
It covers Q3 2026.
### What time does the U.S.
GDP report come out?
The Bureau of Economic Analysis schedules GDP releases for 8:30 AM Eastern Time.
### Why are there three GDP estimates for one quarter?
BEA publishes an advance estimate, a second estimate, and a third estimate as more complete source data become available.
Later annual updates can revise earlier quarters again.
### Is the headline GDP rate annualized?
Yes.
The standard headline quarterly change is seasonally adjusted at an annual rate.
It shows the pace that would result if the quarter-to-quarter change continued for a year.

# Google Cuts Free Gemini to 1 Model Days After Argon [2026]
![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp)
[Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/)
Updated Oct 4, 2026 · 14 min read
Google spent the last week of September showing off its best AI model.
It spent the first week of October taking models away from everyone else.
That split-screen rollout, **Gemini 4 Argon** going out to a small circle of trusted cyber defenders while the free Gemini app gets squeezed down to a single lightweight model, is not two unrelated stories.
It is one strategy, told from two different camera angles, and it says more about where Google thinks the AI business is heading than either headline does on its own.
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, and the model is only reaching the public through a gated channel, Google’s **Fairwind Program**, built for security teams defending networks rather than consumers chatting with an app.
Nine days later, on October 9, Google’s ordinary Gemini app users who do not pay for a subscription lose the ability to pick any model except **Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite**.
Put the two dates next to each other and a pattern appears: Google’s newest, most capable model is being rationed upward toward paying enterprise and security customers, while its oldest commitment, generous free access for casual users, is being rationed downward.
This piece looks at why that pairing matters more than either change alone, who benefits from the split, and what it signals about the rest of the AI market heading into 2027.
## What actually shipped on September 30
Koray Kavukcuoglu, Senior Vice President at Google DeepMind and the company’s chief AI architect, introduced the new model directly: “Today, we’re announcing our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon,” he said, in comments reported by [Anadolu Agency](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/world/google-unveils-frontier-gemini-4-argon-ai-model-begins-rollout-to-cybersecurity-partners/4074335).
He went further in a separate statement carried by [Thurrott](https://www.thurrott.com/a-i/342295/google-makes-new-gemini-4-argon-available-for-cybersecurity-experts), describing the model as “built to sustain deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows,” and adding that Argon “is fundamentally changing the way we work and build at Google.”
The pitch is specific, not generic.
Kavukcuoglu said the model “delivers frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense,” according to the same Thurrott report.
That is a narrower claim than most frontier-model launches make, and the narrowness is the point.
Argon is not being marketed as a better chatbot.
It is being marketed as infrastructure for the kind of professional, high-stakes work that justifies a much higher price tag than a consumer subscription ever could.
## Why Fairwind, and why cyber defenders first
Google did not open Argon to the public or even to its full developer base on day one.
Access is initially limited to participants in the Fairwind Program, Google’s channel for vetted organizations, with an explicit focus on cybersecurity defenders.
Kavukcuoglu explained the reasoning in the same Thurrott-reported remarks: “Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach.” That is a deliberate, security-first rollout strategy, not a capacity constraint dressed up as caution.
The choice to lead with defenders rather than developers in general is notable on its own.
Frontier models carry real dual-use risk: the same reasoning ability that helps a security analyst triage an intrusion can help an attacker write more convincing phishing content or probe for weaknesses faster.
By handing the model first to the people defending networks, Google gets a controlled testing ground with motivated, security-literate users, plus a public-relations case that the model is being used to protect systems before it is widely available at all.
Google has also said it is participating in the U.S.
government’s voluntary process for pre-release model access, which adds a layer of external review most consumer-facing launches never go through.
Google publishes broader detail on its approach to model safety and rollout practices on its [AI blog](https://blog.google/technology/ai/), though the company has not posted a dedicated explainer tying the Argon phased launch directly to the free-tier changes covered below.
## The pricing tells its own story
Alongside the Fairwind rollout, Google published introductory API pricing for Gemini 4 Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted 95% off the standard input rate.
That is a premium price relative to Google’s own smaller models, and it sits in a market where several rivals spent the same few weeks cutting prices rather than raising them.
Shattered.io covered [GPT-6 Sol and Luna launching at roughly 50% below Claude’s pricing](https://shattered.io/gpt-6-sol-luna-pricing-price-war-2026/) and [Anthropic answering with a 20% price cut on Claude Opus 5.5](https://shattered.io/claude-opus-5-5-launch-pricing-2026/), with cached-token costs down 60%.
Argon’s pricing does not chase that race.
It is priced like a specialist tool sold to buyers who care more about capability and vetting than about shaving a few cents off a million tokens.
A simple API call illustrates the gap between how Argon is being sold and how a consumer-tier model is typically accessed.
The structure below is representative of how Fairwind participants are integrating the model into existing security tooling, with the premium per-token cost baked into the call rather than hidden behind a flat subscription fee.
```
POST /v1/models/gemini-4-argon:generateContent Authorization: Bearer FAIRWIND_PROGRAM_KEY Content-Type: application/json { "contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Summarize this intrusion alert and recommend containment steps."}]}], "pricing": {"inputPerMillionTokens": 2.00, "outputPerMillionTokens": 10.00, "cachedInputDiscount": 0.95} }
```
That is a developer-grade, metered pricing model built for organizations with security budgets, not a $4.99-a-month consumer plan.
It is the opposite end of the ladder from what free Gemini app users are being handed nine days later.
## The other half of the split: free users lose two models
Starting October 9, 2026, anyone using the Gemini app without a Google AI subscription will be restricted to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.
They will lose on-demand access to Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro, both of which are currently available to free users on a throttled basis.
Google AI Plus subscribers, who pay $4.99 per month, keep Flash-Lite and Flash but lose Pro.
Only Google AI Pro, at $19.99 per month, and Google AI Ultra retain the full lineup: Flash-Lite, Flash, and Pro, with AI Pro subscribers also gaining access to Deep Think, a mode Google describes as offering maximum parallel reasoning and which was previously reserved for Ultra subscribers only.
The mechanics of that change were first detailed by 9to5Google, which cited an updated Google support document stating plainly: “Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.” That reporting is [available directly from 9to5Google](https://9to5google.com/2026/10/03/gemini-model-limits-oct-26/), and it is the clearest confirmation that this is a model-access restriction, not a usage-limit tweak.
Free users are not simply getting fewer prompts per day on the models they already use.
They are losing the ability to select two of the three models outright.

# All We Know About Google Gemini 4: Release Date, Rumors & What to Expect
By [Lenka Vojtechova](/author/lenka-vojtechova/)  ·  Updated May 20, 2026  ·  11 min read
[AI](/tag/ai/)[Future of AI](/tag/future-of-ai/)[Gemini](/tag/gemini/)[Google](/tag/google/)
![Neon number 4 in a futuristic data tunnel with the text “Everyone’s Talking About Gemini 4 — Here’s What’s Actually Real”.](/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/All-We-Know-About-Gemini-4-release-date-and-confirmed-information-2048x1152-hero.webp)
**Gemini 4 is real, Google has named it, and it is being trained right now.** On **July 21, 2026**, buried in the announcement of a much smaller model, Google wrote that “we have started our most ambitious pre-training run yet, for Gemini 4, and are excited by the progress”.
That is the first time Google has ever confirmed the name in its own words.
Confirmed pre-training is not a release, though, and the gap between the two is where every rumor lives.
There is still no **Gemini 4** model, no documentation and no API access, and Google has attached no date to any of it.
This guide separates what Google has actually said from what the internet has invented.
In it we answer whether **Google Gemini 4** is released yet, what new features and upgrades to expect, and which AI models you should use today until it launches.
## The Key Takeaways
> * **Confirmed, Not Released:** Google confirmed on **July 21, 2026** that pre-training for Gemini 4 has begun, but there is still no documentation and no **API release** for it as of **July 22, 2026**.
> * **Newest Model:** Google shipped **Gemini 3.6 Flash** on **July 21, 2026** at **$1.50 in / $7.50 out** per million tokens.
**Gemini 3.5 Pro**, promised for June, is **still unreleased**.
> * **Evolutionary Steps:** Expect improvements in **agentic workflows**, **video generation**, and **reasoning** rather than just raw token counts.
> * **Use What Works:** You can replicate most anticipated Gemini 4 workflows right now using **Gemini 3.6 Flash**, **Gemini 3.1 Pro**, or **Gemini Omni Flash** in **Fello AI**.
## Current status of Google Gemini 4
From the publisher
Every AI model in one app
Fello AI puts GPT-5.6, Claude 5, Gemini 3.6, Grok 4.5 and more in one native Mac and iPhone app.
[Download now!](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6447705369)
**Gemini 4** is confirmed to exist and confirmed to be in training, but it is not released as a public model in Google’s Gemini API catalogs.
Those are two different things, and most of the confusion online comes from collapsing them.
The fastest way to verify a real launch is to check the official documentation and the dated entries in the official release notes.
As of **July 22, 2026**, there is **no official public documentation** for a model explicitly named “Google Gemini 4” in the developer catalogs or API release notes, and no `gemini-4` string in either the Gemini API or Vertex AI model lists.
If you search through the official model lists today, you will see the newest **Gemini 3.6 Flash** as stable, **Gemini 3.5 Flash** and **Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite**, the **Gemini Omni** series, **Gemini 3.1 Pro** still carrying its `-preview` suffix, and the Gemini 2.5 stable versions.
### What changed recently (Official Timeline)
To understand where we are, look at the recent official release cadence from Google.
| Date | Release | What it added | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Jul 21, 2026** | **Gemini 3.6 Flash** | Same $1.50 input, output cut to $7.50; about 17% fewer output tokens.
Shipped alongside 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.5 Flash Cyber | **Newest** |
| **May 19, 2026** | **Gemini 3.5 Flash + Gemini Omni** | Frontier intelligence at Flash speed; new video creation series | Superseded by 3.6 Flash |
| **Apr 15, 2026** | **Gemini for macOS** | Native desktop app | Live |
| **Feb 19, 2026** | **Gemini 3.1 Pro** | Advanced reasoning for complex tasks | Newest Pro, still preview |
| **Jan 29, 2026** | **Computer Use** | Browser and app control for Gemini 3 preview models | Live |
| **Dec 17, 2025** | **Gemini 3 Flash** | New default model, fast PhD-level reasoning | Superseded |
| **Nov 18, 2025** | **Gemini 3 Pro** | Most intelligent model, higher limits for Pro/Ultra | Superseded |
### Official announcements vs social rumors
The internet is full of speculation.
You might see a post about a **Gemini 4 announcement** on social media, but these are often predictions rather than facts.
Google typically releases new models by updating their technical documentation and publishing a blog post on *The Keyword*.
It is important to understand the difference between a “model update” and a “new generation.” Google frequently pushes updates to existing models without changing the major version number, and the recent jump from **Gemini 3 Pro** to **Gemini 3.1 Pro** to **Gemini 3.5 Flash** is a perfect example.
A new “Gemini 4” generation launch would be accompanied by official documentation updates and a dated release note entry, and would likely align with a major Google product event.
Google naming the model in a blog post, as it did on July 21, is a genuine signal, but it is a signal about the roadmap and not about availability.
### How to check for the release
If you want to know **is Gemini 4 released** for real, do not rely on trending hashtags.
To confirm Gemini 4 availability, rely on official sources.
Consumers should watch the dated **[Gemini release notes](https://gemini.google/release-notes/)**, developers should check the **[API model catalog](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models)** and changelog for new model IDs, and enterprise users should monitor the official enterprise model lists and the **Google AI plans** page.
## Expected features and capabilities
*Note: Below is inference based on Google’s public direction in agents, creation, and computer use (e.g.,* [***Project Mariner (agent prototype)***](https://deepmind.google/models/project-mariner/)*) and the current Gemini roadmap signals, not a leak.*
Even though the model is not out, we can form **grounded expectations** about **Gemini 4 features** based on capabilities currently shipping.
The 3.5 and 3.6 generations raised the bar with frontier intelligence at Flash speed, and Gemini Omni introduced native video generation.
The next step will likely focus on how the AI acts and reasons over longer tasks, moving from “chatbots” to true “agents.”
### Advances in reasoning and context
Users are hoping for a more powerful **Gemini 4 context window**.
Current Gemini API models, 3.6 and 3.5 and 3.1 and 2.5 alike, generally support **1,048,576 input tokens (≈1M)**.
Worth knowing before you plan around that number, Gemini 3.6 Flash retrieves only **54.0%** on GDM-MRCR v2 at the full 1M mark, so a huge window is not the same as reliable recall across it.
Earlier Gemini 1.5 Pro releases supported up to a 2M token context window historically, but today’s competitive focus has shifted to reasoning and tooling.
We expect major improvements in deeper “System 2” thinking where the model takes time to reason before answering, better reliability with fewer hallucinations for enterprise use, and richer **Computer Use** that builds on the [**Gemini 2.5 Computer Use: automate your browser**](/gemini-2-5-computer-use/) tools and the agentic gains already in Gemini 3.5.
### Multimodal upgrades
We also expect **Gemini 4 multimodal** capabilities to push past today’s baseline.
Gemini Omni Flash already accepts image, audio, video, and text input and generates editable video, and Google has since added a cybersecurity-tuned **Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber**, so Gemini 4 will likely extend toward longer-form video, real-time streaming, and tighter integration with agents.
Imagine showing the AI a video of a broken appliance and asking it how to fix it.
A future Gemini 4 agent could watch the video, identify the part, and browse the web to find the replacement without prompting.

# Gemini 4 Launch Window 2026: DeepMind Post-Training Update
[![Fazlur Rahman](/apple-touch-icon-180x180.png)Fazlur Rahman](/blog/author/650f00000000000000000001)8 min read
![Gemini 4 Launch Window 2026: DeepMind Post-Training Update](https://assets.tutorsbot.com/images/pool/gemini-4-launch-window-2026-post-training-8591096d.webp)
**Published September 25, 2026 — Mountain View, Calif.** Google DeepMind's Koray Kavukcuoglu said on Wednesday, September 23, at The Information's AI Agenda Live Summit that Gemini 4 has moved into early post-training.
Google plans to ship the new flagship "much earlier" than year-end 2026 to close the gap with OpenAI's GPT-6 family and Anthropic's Claude 5.5 line.
*Data last verified September 25, 2026 from The Information (via The Verge, Computerworld, Times of India), The Decoder, Google, and Startup Fortune.*
> **At a glance**
>
> * Gemini 4 has entered early post-training, the refinement phase that turns a base model into a shippable product.
> * DeepMind head Koray Kavukcuoglu told The Information on September 23 that Google wants to ship Gemini 4 "much earlier" than year-end.
> * Gemini 4 would be Google's first flagship since the Gemini 3 series shipped in November 2025.
> * No release date, API tier, price, or benchmark has been published; "much earlier" is a signal, not a committed date.
## Quick Answer
**Google DeepMind says Gemini 4 will launch "much earlier" than end of 2026, most likely in October or November 2026 based on the early post-training status, but as of September 25, 2026 there is no firm release date, public API tier, or pricing announced.** The base model has cleared pre-training and is now in the same refinement phase OpenAI used to harden GPT-6 and Anthropic used for Claude Mythos 5.1.
### What post-training actually means
Post-training is the phase that fine-tunes a base model for behaviour, safety, and tool use.
It typically runs for weeks to months depending on the lab's safety bar and how many eval cycles the team runs before launch.
### Why this matters for developers right now
If Gemini 4 ships with strong agentic coding and tool-use benchmarks, Vertex AI customers and AI Studio users should plan a multi-week evaluation cycle before switching any production workload.
Most of the Gemini 3.6 Flash codepath already covers that test path today.
## What Koray Kavukcuoglu said at the AI Agenda Live Summit
**Kavukcuoglu used his first public appearance as DeepMind head to commit to an early Gemini 4 release window and to drop the AGI framing his predecessor favoured.** "Our intention is to [...] as soon as possible [...] release an early post-training output because we see the results and are excited," he told The Information on September 23.
He added that Google would "continue the fast-paced iterations" once the model is out (The Information, September 2026).
Kavukcuoglu took over operational leadership of DeepMind in August 2026 after Demis Hassabis stepped down as CEO.
Hassabis now chairs the unit and serves as Alphabet's chief scientist, the same role Hassabis held throughout the Gemini 1 to 3 era (Startup Fortune, September 2026).
"The conversation of [whether] we achieved AGI or not is not the right conversation," Kavukcuoglu told the summit.
"The conversation is more about are we able to build intelligent agents that we can trust" (The Information, September 2026).
The shift dropped the existential-safety framing Hassabis used in every public appearance through 2024 and 2025.
Alphabet shares slid nearly 5% during the week of the talk on competitive pressure tied to Meta's new Muse AI hardware.
The DeepMind chief's remarks landed with U.S.
equity markets already volatile (Startup Fortune, September 2026).
## Why Gemini 4 is still in post-training, not pre-training
**Pre-training builds the raw model; post-training turns that model into one that behaves reliably for users and tools.** Pre-training on the Gemini 4 dataset is already complete, which is why Sundar Pichai described the run as Google's "most ambitious pre-training run yet" in the Gemini 3.6 Flash announcement on July 21, 2026 (Google blog, July 2026).
Post-training includes supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and tool-use alignment.
Anthropic and OpenAI used the same pipeline to ship Mythos 5.1 and GPT-6 respectively.
Kavukcuoglu told the summit that the team "took a little bit of a step back" to ship faster, less powerful Flash models instead of forcing the Gemini 3.5 Pro release Pichai promised at Google I/O in May 2026.
That promised model was never publicly released (The Information, September 2026).
## How the Gemini 4 timeline compares to OpenAI and Anthropic
**Google has not released a new flagship AI model since the Gemini 3 series shipped in November 2025, which gave OpenAI and Anthropic a free run of 2026.** GPT-6 launched in March 2026, GPT-6 Astra on September 3, GPT-6 Sol and Luna on September 22.
Anthropic shipped Claude Mythos 5.1 on September 1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22.
| Provider | Model | Ship date (2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic | Claude Mythos 5.1 | September 1 |
| Anthropic | Claude Opus 5.5 | September 22 |
| OpenAI | GPT-6 Astra | September 3 |
| OpenAI | GPT-6 Sol | September 22 |
| OpenAI | GPT-6 Luna | September 22 |
| Google | Gemini 3.8 Flash | September 2 |
| Google | Gemini 4 (expected) | Q4 2026 (no firm date) |
*Source: benchlm.ai model release log, official provider announcements, September 2026.*
### What the post-training phase signals about timing
OpenAI moved GPT-6 from initial post-training to general availability in roughly six weeks.
If Google follows a similar pattern, Gemini 4 could appear in late October or early November 2026.
No Google employee has confirmed a date.
## What Gemini 4 needs to ship with at launch
**Developers and enterprise buyers will judge Gemini 4 on coding benchmarks, agentic tool use, and long-context recall, not on press release claims.** Pichai told Alphabet's Q2 earnings call in July 2026 that coding and agentic coding are the two areas where Google needs to close the gap with OpenAI and Anthropic (Alphabet earnings, July 2026).
Expect Google to release Gemini 4 alongside refreshed Gemini API tiers and a Vertex AI rollout.
AI Studio access usually follows within days of an internal launch, depending on safety review outcomes for regulated industries.
If Google wants to match OpenAI's roughly monthly release cadence, the first post-training version will likely be a smaller Gemini 4 variant, with the full Gemini 4 Pro arriving later (The Decoder, September 2026).
## How enterprise teams should plan for Gemini 4 right now
**Plan for Gemini 4 without making it the default until benchmarks and Vertex AI pricing land.** Lock-in risk drops sharply when a new flagship is inside a release window, and most enterprise AI teams treat "much earlier" as a heads-up, not a date.
* Delay long model lock-in contracts until Gemini 4 benchmarks are public.
* Capture a baseline by testing current Gemini 3.8 Flash workloads on Vertex AI.
* Run identical coding and reasoning tasks on Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5.5.
* Track Gemini API pricing for Vertex AI before any production switch.
Until Google publishes prices and benchmarks, treat the "much earlier" statement as a signal that the DevDay-week news cycle will be busy (The Information, September 2026).
## FAQ
*Six short answers on the Gemini 4 launch window in 2026.*
### When is Gemini 4 launching?
Google has not set a public date.
DeepMind head Koray Kavukcuoglu said on September 23, 2026 that Google wants to ship Gemini 4 "much earlier" than end of 2026.
Expect an early preview first, then a wider rollout (The Information, September 2026).

Koray Kavukcuog

# Two killed near Israeli-occupied area in south Lebanon
*Despite a ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Lebanon in June, Israeli attacks continue.*
Save
Share
![One of the volunteers from Lebanon's northernmost province of Akkar and the city of Sidon takes part in an olive-picking initiative in the southern Lebanese village of Jibshit near Nabatieh on October 11, 2026, in a show of solidarity with Southern Lebanon and its farmers whose crops and livelihoods were affected by the war.](/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/afp_6acbe7caf38c-1791748043.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
A worker helps with the annual olive harvest in the southern Lebanese village of Jebchit near Nabatieh on October 11, 2026 [AFP]
By AFP
Published On 11 Oct 202611 Oct 2026
Two men have been killed in southern Lebanon’s Bint Jbeil district while taking part in an annual olive harvest, according to Lebanese state media and local authorities, as attacks by Israel continue.
One of the men died Sunday in the village of Froun from a munition left behind by recent fighting and the other in Yater as a result of Israeli shelling that “targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest”, according to the official National News Agency (NNA).
## Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
* list 1 of 3[Lebanese are watching Israel’s upcoming election, but few expect change](/news/2026/9/29/lebanese-are-watching-israels-upcoming-election-but-few-expect-change)
* list 2 of 3[Syria denies officials held ‘secret’ talks with Hezbollah in Turkiye](/news/2026/10/1/syria-denies-officials-held-secret-talks-with-hezbollah-in-turkiye)
* list 3 of 3[‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days](/news/2026/9/30/dire-situation-lebanese-prisoners-on-hunger-strike-for-18-days)
end of list
The Lebanese army blamed Israeli tank fire and called the ongoing attacks “a flagrant breach of existing agreements”.
Afterwards, the Yater municipality urged residents “to avoid the outskirts of the town and refrain from crossing the earthen barrier separating some unsafe neighbourhoods” for fear of Israeli attacks.
In Froun, the NNA reported that “a foreign object” left over from previous Israeli operations exploded and killed the man, who was an engineer, as he and others tended their trees.
The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.
The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for “the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village”, Bazzi said.
## Displaced people
Since an [agreement](/news/2026/6/26/what-is-the-framework-agreement-signed-by-israel-and-lebanon) between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, violence in the south has lessened, but not [stopped](/news/2026/9/18/two-injured-by-israeli-shelling-as-troops-advance-in-southern-lebanon).
Lebanon was pulled into conflict on March 2, when Hezbollah struck Israel in support of Tehran during the US-Israel war on Iran.
Subsequently, Israel launched a bombing [campaign](/news/2026/4/30/civilians-or-hezbollah-who-did-israel-hit-on-lebanons-black-wednesday) and a ground invasion that authorities say have killed more than 4,300.
Advertisement
In August, Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam [accused](/news/2026/8/13/israeli-strikes-in-south-lebanon-a-violation-of-international-law-pm) Israel of intentionally targeting homes and civilian infrastructure across the country.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) recorded nearly 350,000 internally displaced people in late August, a sign of the worsening displacement [crisis.](/features/2026/9/13/how-israels-destruction-of-south-lebanon-is-making-displacement-permanent)
![One of the volunteers from Lebanon's northernmost province of Akkar and the city of Sidon takes part in an olive-picking initiative in the southern Lebanese village of Jibshit near Nabatieh on October 11, 2026, in a show of solidarity with Southern Lebanon and its farmers whose crops and livelihoods were affected by the war.](/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/afp_6acbe742b945-1791747906.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C514&quality=80)
One of the volunteers from Lebanon’s northernmost province of Akkar and the city of Sidon takes part in an olive-picking initiative in the southern Lebanese village of Jebchit near Nabatieh on October 11, 2026 [AFP]
Volunteers from the nearby town of Jebchit and locals came to help their southern neighbours with the harvest in an act of solidarity.
“From north to south, one people and one land,” said organiser Ahmad Chahhal.

JERSUALEM — The Israel Defense Forces struck 100,000 targets over three years of war on multiple fronts, the Israeli military said in a release of [data](https://www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/israel-at-war/idf-data-over-three-years-of-war/) marking the third anniversary of the Oct.
7, 2023 terrorist attacks.
The IDF does not define what a “target” means in this context, but the size of the figure, which includes strikes in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Iran, shows the breadth of conflict Israel has waged since the Hamas terrorist attacks upended the region.
The data release also included information on new units formed during the war and the changes in IDF reserve forces, as Israel has had to adapt its military structures on the fly.
Unsurprisingly, the majority of strikes were in Gaza, where the IDF claims it has struck 65,000 targets, with around 30,000 of these in just the first three months of the conflict — a pace that shows in the widespread destruction of buildings and displacement of the population that was evident quickly after the war began.
Outside Gaza, the IDF said Israel also struck 28,000 targets in Lebanon and Syria, as well as 4,500 in Iran and 80 in Yemen.
The Iran targets were struck during a 12-day conflict in June 2025, as well as an exchange of fire on Feb.
28, 2026.
Syria, for its part, has become more [outspoken](https://sana.sy/en/politics/2341593/) in recent weeks about what it says are Israeli [violations](https://sana.sy/en/politics/2348050/) within Syrian territory near the Golan.
The IDF has also increased its tempo of operations in the West Bank.
It says it has confiscated 3,800 weapons and arrested “45,000 wanted individuals.”
The IDF believes it has eliminated four Hamas military branch heads, as well as 17 Hamas brigade commanders, 60 battalion commanders and 300 company commanders.
This means most of Hamas’ five brigades and 24 battalions have seen their commanders eliminated several times in the war.
A total of 970 Israeli soldiers and service personnel have fallen in the war.
This is in addition to more than 800 civilians killed on Oct.
7.
Overall Palestinian casualty figures were not included in the new dataset, but Israel has [reportedly](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/30/israel-military-gaza-death-toll-broadly-accurate) accepted assertions by Gaza’s health ministry that over 70,000 have been killed.
The ministry [does not distinguish](https://apnews.com/article/israel-gaza-iran-israel-yemen-september-27-2026-96b100178557a28f51e2ad4f74539699) between civilians and militants.
Additionally, the new figures show that Israel’s missile defenses were sorely tested over the last three years: The IDF said that approximately 31,540 projectiles were launched at Israel from multiple fronts, including approximately 10,200 from Gaza, 20,000 from Lebanon, 1,200 from Iran, 50 from Syria, and 90 from Yemen.
While the IDF does not release interception rates, during the recent conflict with Iran [local reports](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/iaf-says-failure-to-intercept-two-separate-iranian-missiles-last-night-in-south-is-coincidental/) put the success rate at 92 percent.
The new data are the latest in several data sets that the IDF released throughout the war.
The IDF’s first data set was [released](https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2024/01/israel-releases-data-on-three-months-of-fighting-in-gaza.php) after three months of conflict, but a link to its [appears](https://www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/idf-press-releases-regarding-the-hamas-israel-war/january-24-pr/war-against-hamas-interim-data/operational-targets/) to have been taken down.
The Israeli Air Force [said](https://www.iaf.org.il/9737-61798-he/IAF.aspx) that by February 2024 it had struck 31,000 targets, and the IDF released [data](https://www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/idf-press-releases-israel-at-war/april-24-press-releases/war-against-hamas-6-months-operational-update/) sets for six months of war in April 2024 and nine months of [conflict](https://www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/idf-press-releases-israel-at-war/july-24-pr/operational-summary-of-idf-activity-over-the-past-9-months-in-gaza/) in July 2024.
However, since then the military appeared to stop releasing this type of data until this week’s milestone.
***Breaking Defense’s team has been on the ground during the conflicts.
Read some of their personal reflections here:***
* [In South Lebanon, empty villages, ruined crops and fears of what comes next](https://breakingdefense.com/2024/06/in-south-lebanon-empty-villages-ruined-crops-and-fears-of-what-comes-next/) (June 2024)
* [In Northern Israel, emptied villages and talk of war in Lebanon](https://breakingdefense.com/2024/06/in-northern-israel-emptied-villages-and-talk-of-war-in-lebanon/) (June 2024)

## Modernizing The Military
The data release also emphasized how the war has caused major changes within the Israeli military.
One lesson is that the IDF needs more ground forces to confront threats on multiple fronts, a reversal of  a decade in which Israel had been reducing the ground forces and focusing more on technological innovation and small units.
The IDF notes that it created several new brigades and divisions, including a new Mountain [Brigade](https://breakingdefense.com/2024/04/new-idf-mountain-brigade-to-bolster-israels-northern-defenses/) on the northern border and a new division to [coordinate](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/03/inside-the-idfs-newest-military-division-securing-the-jordan-valley/) defense of the Jordan Valley.
The IDF also [expanded](https://breakingdefense.com/2024/04/in-ongoing-war-idf-beefs-up-armored-corps-with-new-tank-companies/) its armored corps with new regular service tank companies.
In addition, the IDF said it “has worked to expand its personnel pool and establish new frameworks in accordance with operational needs that have emerged during combat.” This includes new unspecified units within the intelligence and air defense sectors.

### October 2026 Monthly Forecast
#### Lebanon
##### **Expected Council Action**
In October, Security Council members are expected to receive their semi-annual briefing in closed consultations on the Secretary-General’s report on the implementation of [resolution 1559](https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/un-documents/document/lebanon-sres1559.php).
Adopted in 2004, the resolution called for the withdrawal of foreign forces from Lebanon, the disarmament of all militias, and the extension of government control over the whole Lebanese territory.
Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo is the anticipated briefer.
Council members are also likely to continue considering options for possible arrangements after the termination of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) to support the continued implementation of resolution 1701, which in 2006 called for a cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.
This follows the Council’s unanimous adoption in August 2025 of [resolution 2790](https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/un-documents/document/s-res-2790.php), which extended UNIFIL’s mandate for a final time until 31 December and directed the mission to begin an orderly drawdown and full withdrawal from that date, “and within one year”.
##### **Key Recent Developments**
On 26 June, Lebanon, Israel, and the US signed a [Trilateral Framework](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/06/trilateral-framework-between-the-united-states-of-america-the-state-of-israel-and-the-republic-of-lebanon/) intended to chart a way to end the latest escalation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah, which began on 2 March shortly after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February.
During the hostilities, Israel [deployed](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/idf-publishes-fresh-map-of-south-lebanon-deployment-says-it-wont-be-withdrawing-yet/) to an area of up to 10 kilometres in Lebanese territory.
Despite the Trilateral Framework and [subsequent](https://www.agenzianova.com/a/6a563505044e42.39908512/7604768/2026-07-14/libano-israele-iniziato-a-roma-nuovo-ciclo-di-negoziati-presso-ambasciata-usa) follow-up [negotiations](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/08/04/lebanon-and-israel-hold-new-round-of-direct-talks-in-rome-to-discuss-hezbollah-disarming), hostilities have continued in southern Lebanon.
In the Trilateral Framework, Israel and Lebanon committed to a process by which the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) will “restore effective sovereign authority over all Lebanese territory, pending the verified disarmament of non-state armed groups and dismantlement of associated infrastructure, enabling the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to progressively redeploy out of the Lebanese territory”.
According to the framework and its [security annex](https://www.timesofisrael.com/eventual-idf-redeployment-from-lebanon-full-text-of-israel-lebanon-deal-security-annex/), the LAF would gradually assume security responsibilities for “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, following the verification by “a mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” of the absence of non-state armed groups and associated weapons and infrastructure in these areas.
However, a decision on which entity, state, or states may assume this third-party function has yet to be reached.
The prospects of the US-mediated negotiations between Lebanon and Israel remain unclear.
Following two rounds of talks in Rome over the summer, a further round anticipated for mid-September was [postponed](https://www.haaretz.com/middle-east-news/lebanonnews/2026-09-12/ty-article/israel-lebanon-talks-in-rome-reportedly-postponed-to-october/000001a0-9436-d219-a3ed-bdfe9b3c0000) until October.
The latest round of negotiations, which took place in August, [reportedly](https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2026-09-13/israel-and-lebanon-to-meet-in-rome-in-october-us-state-department-official-says) ended without reaching agreement on key issues.
On 28 August, Council members held closed consultations on Lebanon at France’s request in order to begin considering possible arrangements following the termination of UNIFIL.
The consultations were also prompted by a deterioration in conditions on the ground.
In a 3 September [update](https://press.un.org/en/2026/db260903.doc.htm), Spokesperson for the Secretary-General Stéphane Dujarric said that while incidents decreased following the signing of the Framework Agreement, UNIFIL recorded an increase in violence in August, with the mission recording daily violations by Israel of Lebanese airspace, as well as airstrikes, ground activities, and naval operations, and extensive Israeli military presence north of the Blue Line, in violation of resolution 1701 and of Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He added that UNIFIL peacekeepers had reported the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, the construction of new infrastructure, and other engineering works, with the presence of individuals appearing to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of the military operations.
The update noted that peacekeepers last detected Hezbollah projectiles on 21 June.
IDF military operations in southern Lebanon have continued in September, including by taking “operational control” of the Ali al‑Taher ridge, a strategic position near the city of Nabatiyeh, [destroying](https://www.naharnet.com/stories/en/322411-israel-blows-up-ali-al-taher-tunnels-with-1-100-tons-of-explosives) tunnels used by Hezbollah inside the ridge, and through airstrikes and extensive demolitions affecting residential areas.
In an 8 September [statement](https://press.un.org/en/2026/sgsm23267.doc.htm), the Secretary-General condemned the “mounting civilian casualties, including women and children killed and injured in the intensifying attacks, the distress and displacement caused by the evacuation orders, and the scenes of massive destruction and devastation”.
The statement said that the Secretary-General was “particularly alarmed by reported Israeli strikes affecting hospitals, healthcare workers and public institutions, as well as restrictions on humanitarian access”.
Successive UN [updates](https://press.un.org/en/2026/db260925.doc.htm) in September continued to report IDF activity in southern Lebanon, including the dropping of explosive-filled [jerrycans](https://press.un.org/en/2026/db260917.doc.htm) within UNIFIL’s area of operations and [denials](https://press.un.org/en/2026/db260921.doc.htm) of freedom of movement.
Attention is increasingly turning to arrangements for the period following UNIFIL’s termination.
One possibility is the initiative for an “international coalition to support Lebanon” after the mission’s closure, [announced](https://www.elysee.fr/en/emmanuel-macron/2026/06/25/franco-italian-joint-statement#:~:text=We%20strongly%20support%20UNIFIL%20and%20underline%20its%20essential%20role%20in%20consolidating%20progress%20following%20the%20ceasefire.%20We%20will%20collaborate%20together%20on%20post%2DUNIFIL%20reflections%20co%2Dleading%20an%20international%20coalition%20to%20support%20Lebanon%20in%20a%20post%2DUNIFIL%20context.) on 25 June by French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
While French and Italian authorities have [stressed](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/moyen-orient/20260625-liban-la-france-et-l-italie-veulent-mettre-en-place-une-coalition-multinationale-pour-succ%C3%A9der-%C3%A0-la-finul) that the initiative would aim to reinforce Lebanon’s sovereignty and help prevent a security vacuum in southern Lebanon, its precise contours are yet to be defined.
In parallel, the EU has [advanced](https://www.euractiv.com/news/eu-steps-up-planning-for-post-unifil-mission-in-lebanon/) planning for a possible civilian-military mission aimed at advising and training the LAF and Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces.

# Ceasefire Begins in Israel-Hezbollah War
![Staff Writer with AFP](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/e01218cab909a9717fb48d141e90f60940b1803f4ca436a4a237a24b6ea77668?s=80&d=blank&r=g) by [Staff Writer with AFP](https://theglobepost.com/author/staff-writer/)

in [National](https://theglobepost.com/category/national/)

Rescuers sift through the rubble at the scene of an Israeli strike that targets Beirut's southern suburbs.
Photo: Fadel Itani/NurPhoto via AFP](https://theglobepost.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Lebanon-strike.jpg)
[Share on Facebook](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Ftheglobepost.com%2F2024%2F11%2F26%2Fhezbollah-israel-ceasefire%2F)[Share on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Ceasefire+Begins+in+Israel-Hezbollah+War&url=https%3A%2F%2Ftheglobepost.com%2F2024%2F11%2F26%2Fhezbollah-israel-ceasefire%2F)
A ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon took effect on Wednesday after more than a year of fighting that has killed thousands of people.
The truce, which began at 4:00 am (0200 GMT), should bring to a halt a war that has forced tens of thousands of people in Israel and hundreds of thousands more in Lebanon to flee their homes.
The war has seen swathes of Lebanon pounded by air strikes, and [Israeli troops deployed across the border](https://thedefensepost.com/2024/09/30/israel-ground-raids-south-lebanon/) to battle Hezbollah militants.
It began with Hezbollah launching cross-border strikes in support of its Palestinian ally Hamas following [its October 7, 2023 attack on Israel](https://thedefensepost.com/2023/10/07/israel-gaza-war-hamas-attack/).
US President **Joe Biden** announced the ceasefire agreement on Tuesday, as Israeli Prime Minister **Benjamin Netanyahu** said his ministers had agreed to a halt.
The United States is Israel’s key ally and military backer, and Biden hailed the deal as “good news” and a “new start” for Lebanon.
Netanyahu thanked Biden for his involvement in brokering the deal, and said it would allow Israel to focus on Hamas in Gaza and Iran.
Under the terms of the Lebanon truce, Israel will maintain “full” freedom to act against Hezbollah should the Iran-backed group pose any new threat, Netanyahu said.
Lebanon says at least 3,823 people have been killed in the country since exchanges of fire began in October 2023, most of them in the past several weeks when [Israel escalated its campaign against Hezbollah](https://thedefensepost.com/2024/10/16/israel-pounds-hezbollah-strongholds/).
On the Israeli side, the hostilities with Hezbollah have killed at least 82 soldiers and 47 civilians, authorities say.
The hours before the truce took effect were some of the most violent in the war.
Israel conducted a spate of strikes on the heart of the Lebanese capital on Tuesday, while Hezbollah claimed attacks on northern Israel after the truce was announced.
Hezbollah did not participate in any direct talks for the truce, with Lebanese parliamentary speaker Nabih Berri mediating on its behalf.
It has yet to formally comment on the truce.

# Israel Hezbollah April 2026: Ceasefire Status & Outlook.
Israel-Hezbollah April 2026: ceasefire holding partially, southern Lebanon damage, UNIFIL status, Hezbollah weakening, reconstruction.
**BEIRUT, April 28, 2026.** The Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire signed in November 2024 has, against most expert predictions, survived eighteen months of pressure, the death of Hassan Nasrallah, the elevation of a new Hezbollah secretary-general who lacks his predecessor’s authority, the formation of a Lebanese government for the first time in over two years, and now the ongoing eight-week US-Israel-Iran war that has put the entire regional security architecture under stress.
As of late April 2026, the ceasefire is holding partially.
From the southern Lebanese village of Kfar Kila on the Blue Line, the war is over but not finished, the reconstruction has begun but not arrived, and the political map of the Lebanese south is being rewritten in real time by men in Beirut, Riyadh, Tel Aviv, and Washington who do not all share the same map.
The structural picture as of April 2026 will not, at least not in the next 30 to 60 days.
The text built on the architecture of UN Security Council Resolution 1701 from 2006 and added an explicit timetable for a phased Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon coupled with a phased Lebanese Armed Forces deployment to fill the vacuum, supported by an expanded UNIFIL presence.
Hezbollah was, in the formal text, a non-party — the agreement was struck between the Lebanese state and the Israeli government, with Hezbollah’s compliance an implicit but unwritten condition.
The Lebanese government under President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam wants the ceasefire to hold for the simple reason that war means more displacement, more destruction, and the death of the reconstruction project that is the new government’s principal domestic justification.
Lebanese deaths exceeded 4,000 by the time the guns paused, with the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health placing approximately 1,200 of those as Hezbollah fighters killed in the southern Lebanon ground campaign and the IDF airstrikes on the southern suburbs of Beirut, Dahiyeh, and the Beqaa.
